questions.prompt: The CAP theorem states that during a network partition, a distributed system must choose between:

options.text: Consistency and availability
Latency and throughput
Consistency and partition tolerance
Availability and durability

questions.explanation: Partitions are a fact of networks, not a design option, so P is not really negotiable. The real decision is whether a partitioned node refuses requests to stay consistent, or answers and risks divergence.

options.text: All reads return the most recent write immediately
If writes stop, all replicas eventually converge to the same value
Reads are always served by the primary node
Writes are never lost under any circumstances

questions.explanation: It is a liveness property with no bound on when convergence happens, and it says nothing about what intermediate reads return. That is precisely why stronger models such as read-your-writes are layered on top.

questions.prompt: Why is idempotency important for operations retried over an unreliable network?

options.text: It makes each retry faster than the last
It removes the need for acknowledgements
It guarantees the operation succeeds on the first attempt
Applying the operation more than once has the same effect as applying it once

questions.explanation: A client that times out cannot tell whether the request was lost or the response was. Safe retries therefore require the server to deduplicate, usually via a client-supplied idempotency key.

questions.prompt: In a quorum system with N replicas, a write quorum W and a read quorum R, what condition guarantees a read sees the latest write?

options.text: R + W > N
R = W
R + W = N
R + W < N

questions.explanation: If the read and write sets must overlap, at least one replica in every read has seen the latest write. Choosing W = N and R = 1 favours fast reads; W = 1 and R = N favours fast writes.

questions.prompt: Why is two-phase commit considered a blocking protocol?

options.text: It requires all participants to be on the same machine
Participants that have voted to commit cannot proceed if the coordinator fails
It locks the entire database during the prepare phase
It can only commit one transaction per second

questions.explanation: A prepared participant has promised it can commit and must hold its locks until told the outcome. If the coordinator dies at that moment, participants are stuck — which is what three-phase commit and consensus protocols address.

questions.prompt: What problem do vector clocks solve that physical timestamps do not?

options.text: They guarantee a total order of all events
They keep every machine's clock synchronised
They capture causal ordering without relying on synchronised clocks
They compress event history for storage

questions.explanation: Machine clocks drift and skew, so a later wall-clock stamp does not imply a later event. Vector clocks track causality directly and can detect genuinely concurrent updates that need conflict resolution.

questions.prompt: The saga pattern maintains consistency across microservices by:

options.text: Replicating every service's database to every other service
Deferring all writes until the workflow completes
Holding a distributed lock for the duration of the workflow
Splitting the workflow into local transactions, each with a compensating action on failure

questions.explanation: Sagas accept that a single ACID transaction across services is impractical. Each step commits locally, and failure triggers compensating actions to unwind earlier steps — so intermediate states are visible.

questions.prompt: A leader election protocol such as Raft requires a majority quorum. Why does this prevent split brain?

options.text: Two disjoint majorities cannot exist simultaneously in one cluster
Majorities make elections finish faster
It guarantees the fastest node is always elected
It removes the need for heartbeats

questions.explanation: Any two majorities of the same set must share at least one member, and that member will not vote for two leaders in the same term. So a partition can produce at most one leader.

questions.prompt: What is the fundamental difficulty a heartbeat-based failure detector faces?

options.text: Heartbeats consume most of the network bandwidth
A slow node and a failed node are indistinguishable from the outside
Heartbeats cannot be sent over TCP
Failed nodes continue sending heartbeats

questions.explanation: In an asynchronous network there is no timeout that separates crashed from merely slow. A short timeout declares healthy nodes dead; a long one delays recovery — the trade-off cannot be eliminated.

questions.prompt: Which statement about strong consistency versus eventual consistency is correct?

options.text: Eventual consistency always uses less storage
Eventual consistency guarantees lower durability
Strong consistency generally costs more latency because of cross-node coordination
Strong consistency removes the need for replication

questions.explanation: Making every reader observe the newest write requires nodes to agree before responding, which costs at least one round trip. Eventual consistency answers locally and reconciles afterwards, trading correctness guarantees for speed.
